passages.t: ‘Flee like a bird to your mountain’, and the LORD on His throne
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. Of David” (verse 1). Then the psalm's first words, and its whole answer: “In the LORD I take refuge” (verse 1).

Friends are giving advice. “Flee like a bird to your mountain!” they say (verse 1). The wicked have their arrows ready “to shoot from the shadows at the upright in heart” (verse 2). And they end with a question that sounds like despair: “If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (verse 3).

The psalmist does not run. He looks up instead. “The LORD is in His holy temple; the LORD is on His heavenly throne” (verse 4). God is not asleep. “His eyes are watching closely; they examine the sons of men” (verse 4). He tests both the righteous and the wicked, and “His soul hates the lover of violence” (verse 5).

The psalm ends with judgment on the violent and a promise to the upright: “For the LORD is righteous; He loves justice. The upright will see His face” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
This is a psalm of trust. It has no complaint to God at all. It argues with frightened friends.

The advice is not foolish. In the hill country of Israel, people in danger did run to the mountains, with their caves and rough ground. David himself hid there when Saul hunted him (1 Samuel 23:14). A bird darting up to the heights was a natural picture of escape.

The key line is verse 3. ‘The foundations’ most likely means the order that holds a society together: fair courts, honest dealing, protection for the weak. When that order cracks, good people feel there is nothing left to do. The psalm answers with another foundation. Before the earth's courts there is a throne in heaven, and it has not moved.

‘Fiery coals and sulfur’ in verse 6 recalls the fall of Sodom (Genesis 19:24). On God's hatred of evil, see the note on Psalm 5.
passages.later:
The hope of verse 7, to see God's face, runs through the whole Bible. Jesus said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5:8). The last chapter of the Bible says of God's people: “They will see His face” (Revelation 22:4).

Jesus also spoke to people tempted to run in fear. “Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28). Hebrews speaks of “an unshakable kingdom” (Hebrews 12:28), a foundation that does not crack.
passages.asks:
The psalm does not say running is always wrong. David ran from Saul more than once. It asks where your refuge really is when the ground shakes. Is it a place you can flee to, or the God who is still on his throne?

When the news makes you ask ‘What can the righteous do?’, pray verse 4 slowly. Then do the next right thing in front of you. You can pray this psalm for anyone who feels the foundations giving way.
